A .gitmodules line that the VM writes, such as ignore = none, makes git status enter a submodule again, and git add -A, git add -u, git describe --dirty, git diff-index, git diff-files, git fetch and git pull enter one whatever the setting says, as does --ignore-submodules on the command line.

A VM that was made strict shows as on at once, in devvm ls, devvm git-protect and its --json, and its locks stay as they are while it runs. The first time devvm finds it stopped, at a launch, at devvm stop, or at devvm clone on, or when devvm undoes a devvm clone off that didn’t finish, devvm takes diff.ignoreSubmodules = all out of the .git/config of the folder’s own repo and of each nested repo the VM protected, unlocking each file for the moment and locking it again. Then it records the VM as on and says so once, unless you chose devvm git-protect off while it ran, which it applies next. devvm git-protect on and off and devvm rm take the setting out the same way, without saying so.

devvm leaves the setting where it can’t tell that it set it, and names what it leaves:

  • strict doesn’t record a value that the setting had before it sets its own, so devvm can’t put one back. It takes out only the value all, so a value that you set since, such as none or dirty, stays.
  • devvm leaves the setting alone in a repo whose .git isn’t the one it recorded, because strict never set it there: a .git that the VM replaced, which devvm names, a nested repo that it finds for the first time at that check, and every repo of a VM it has no record of, such as one that devvm adopt moved. When such a config sets all, devvm names it once.
  • On a Linux host that watches .git, it also leaves a config that changed since the check read it, which the next check names.
  • If git can’t change a config, devvm names it, and git status and git diff on this machine go on skipping that repo’s submodules until you take the setting out yourself.
  • A .git/config that another VM’s protection also keeps locked keeps the setting, because unlocking it would let that VM change the file if it runs, and devvm names the file and that VM at each launch that finds this VM stopped. devvm takes the setting out at such a check once the other VM no longer keeps the file locked.

To take the setting out of a repo yourself, if you didn’t set it:

devvm stop # in this VM's folder, and in the other VM's when another VM locks the file too
devvm git-protect off
git config --file .git/config --unset-all diff.ignoreSubmodules '^all$' # in that repo
devvm git-protect on # lock .git again as it is then

Stop both VMs when another VM keeps the file locked too, because a running VM could change the file while it’s unlocked, and a launch into a running VM locks nothing. In that case, run chflags nouchg .git/config on macOS in place of devvm git-protect off, and the next launch of either VM finds it stopped and locks the file again, and on Linux the other VM’s watch names the change.

When devvm reports .git

Every launch of an existing VM, and devvm stop, check .git again, and devvm reports what it finds there that it didn’t lock. When it names one of these, check it before you run git in the folder, because git on this machine would run what the VM put there:

  • A repo that appeared in the folder after its VM was made, the folder’s own or a nested one. devvm locks it from then on, but if you didn’t make it, check its hooks and config.
  • A submodule that appeared with its git folder in the project folder. devvm locks it from then on, but git on this machine may already have run what its config and hooks say (not covered), so if you didn’t add it, check them.
  • A nested repo that’s gone or moved, which the VM could have moved aside to put another in its place.
  • Hooks in a folder devvm hadn’t locked, because the folder wasn’t there to lock or belongs to a new submodule.
  • A submodule whose git folder isn’t one. The VM can name any folder in the project as a submodule’s git folder, such as your src, so devvm locks nothing in a folder that doesn’t look like a git folder, and names the submodule instead.
  • A path that’s a symlink or under one. devvm never locks anything through a symlink, because the VM could point one at a file elsewhere on this machine, so it leaves that path unlocked.
  • A path that moved while devvm locked it. devvm leaves it unlocked and takes the lock off wherever it landed, so check .git.

How it works › .git protection lists every check.

Nested repos

A folder can hold git repos of its own besides its submodules, such as ws/repo-a and ws/repo-b in a folder ws, whether ws is a repo itself or only a folder of repos. The VM can write all of them, and git on this machine runs what their .git holds when you run git there, so devvm protects each one it finds as it protects the folder’s own .git: it locks them on macOS, makes them read-only in the VM on Linux, and watches them on a Linux host that can’t lock. It finds them this way:

  • When: when it creates the VM, at each launch that finds the VM stopped and at devvm stop. A launch into a running VM doesn’t look again, and it doesn’t check the nested repos either, so they’re checked at the next launch that finds the VM stopped, or at devvm stop.
  • Where: up to four folders below the project folder, for anything named .git (on macOS, .GIT as well). It doesn’t look in the folders that package managers and build tools fill, node_modules, vendor, .venv, __pycache__ and .terraform, nor in a folder on another disk.
  • How many: it protects the first 100 it finds and names the rest, at every check.

What still works and what doesn’t is the same in a nested repo as in the folder’s own: git config, git remote add and hook installers fail there on macOS, so run them with protection off. devvm keeps protecting a nested repo for as long as anything is at its .git, even when that .git no longer looks like a repo’s, because the VM can change it back at any time.

When you don’t need the VM to write your working trees, devvm --clone in a folder of repos keeps the VM out of all of them instead:

cd ws && devvm --clone # a VM with its own clone of each repo you choose, mounting none of them
devvm clone fetch # bring the VM's work back

The VM gets a clone of each repo you choose, at the same path, and mounts nothing of this machine, so it can’t reach any repo’s working tree or .git here, and none of what this page describes applies to it (folders of repos). You get its work back with devvm clone fetch.

devvm can’t protect a repo before it has found it, so when you run git in a folder of a VM’s project while the VM runs, the protection holds only for the repos devvm has already found:

  • A repo the VM makes in the folder while it runs, by cloning one or by making a .git in a folder of yours, is git’s repo for that folder from the moment it’s there: your git status in the folder, and the shell prompts and editors that run git as you open it, run what its config says.
  • devvm names such a repo only at the next launch that finds the VM stopped, or at devvm stop, with the settings in its config and the hooks that run programs, and then locks it as it is, so check what it names before you run git there.
  • A repo the VM makes more than four folders down, or in a folder devvm doesn’t look in, is never named, only counted where devvm walks the folder for set-id files on Linux.
  • On Linux the VM can also move a nested repo’s folder aside and put another repo in its place while it runs, which devvm names only if it’s still in place when the VM stops (Linux hosts).

Bare repos

git also takes a folder shaped like a git folder, with a HEAD, objects and refs, for a bare repo, and its config can name a work tree, so git run in a folder below one uses it, core.fsmonitor and all. The VM can make one anywhere in the folder. devvm names the ones it finds up to four folders down that aren’t a repo’s own git folder, and devvm doctor gives a tip when git on this machine takes a bare repo it isn’t told to use. git 2.38 and newer can refuse that: git config --global safe.bareRepository explicit makes git use a bare repo only when you name it, with --git-dir or GIT_DIR. devvm only checks the setting, and never changes your git config.

VMs an earlier devvm made

A VM that an earlier devvm made protects only the folder’s own repo. The first time devvm finds nested repos in its folder, it names them once and tells you to run devvm git-protect on, which protects them all from then on. Until you do, devvm names each nested repo it finds that it hadn’t named before.

Two VMs, one repo

A nested repo can have a VM of its own, and then two VMs protect it. On macOS, the flag that locks it is the same for both, so devvm rm or devvm git-protect off for one VM leaves locked what the other VM still protects, and names that VM. Run devvm git-protect off for the other VM too when you want the locks off. When devvm can’t read another VM’s state, it leaves locked what that VM may protect, and names the state to fix. On Linux, each VM has its own read-only view, so each protects the repo from its own VM.

A nested repo devvm stopped protecting, because it’s gone or moved, keeps its locks until devvm takes them off with the rest, at devvm rm or devvm git-protect off. When it’s no longer in the folder, devvm can’t find it to unlock it, so it names it, and chflags -R nouchg on its .git/hooks and .git/config takes the locks off.

Not covered

The lock covers .git, and the VM can still put things elsewhere that git on this machine runs. devvm tells you about each of these, so read what it reports before you run git in the folder, and use --clone for a repo you don’t trust.

  • Hooks in the working tree, such as husky’s .husky/ with core.hooksPath=.husky, or an absolute path into the project folder. The VM can edit them, and they run on this machine. devvm warns about them when it creates the VM.
  • What the locked files hand over to the project folder, which is an include.path or includeIf.*.path that leads into it, or a hook that’s a symlink into it. The VM can edit those files, and git on this machine reads or runs them. devvm warns about them when it creates the VM, and on a launch after they change.
  • Submodules whose git folder is outside the project. devvm can’t lock that folder, because another project’s VM may write it, and git status on this machine reads its config. devvm names these submodules when it creates the VM.
  • A submodule the VM adds. The VM writes .git/index, because it has to in order to commit, so it can add a submodule with a git folder of its own anywhere in the project folder. Whenever git on this machine enters that submodule, it reads the submodule’s config and runs its hooks, so its core.fsmonitor runs on this machine. git status, git diff, git add -A and git describe --dirty all enter it, and so do the shell prompts and editors that run them. devvm names the submodule and locks its git folder only at devvm stop or at the next launch that finds the VM stopped (when devvm reports .git).
  • A replaced .git. The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, or point git at another config. devvm reports this on each launch but doesn’t undo it (what a lock can’t stop).
  • Some of the git repos nested in the folder. devvm protects each repo it finds below the project folder (nested repos), but not one more than four folders down, one in a folder that a package manager fills, such as node_modules, one on another disk, or one past the first 100. It doesn’t lock the git folder that a nested repo’s .git file names unless that’s another repo’s that devvm locks, and a git folder outside the project folder it can’t lock at all. The VM can set core.fsmonitor in such a repo’s config, and your next git status there runs it. devvm names the ones it finds and doesn’t protect, and counts those on other disks, so check them before you run git there, or move them out of the folder.
  • A repo the VM makes while it runs, and a bare repo it makes. git on this machine uses either as soon as it’s there, and devvm finds it only once the VM stops (nested repos).

Linux hosts

On Linux, devvm runs each VM’s QEMU in a user namespace of its own, without root, and there it makes the paths that macOS’s flag would lock read-only: the hooks and config of .git and of its submodules, and the rest of what’s locked. The VM reaches the project folder only through QEMU, so root in the VM gets Read-only file system when it writes one of them, and Device or resource busy when it renames or removes one, or renames .git itself.

  • A nested repo’s own folder isn’t pinned, so the VM can still rename the folder, .git and all, and put another repo in its place, which devvm reports at the next check as a replaced .git.
  • Nothing changes on this machine: your own git commands write .git/config as usual, and the read-only view ends when the VM stops.
  • devvm git-protect works as it does on macOS, and a change to a running VM’s protection applies at its next start.

Warning

Start VMs with devvm. A VM that limactl start starts runs without the read-only view, and so does one whose view went for another reason, so each launch of a running VM, and devvm stop, check that the VM still can’t rename .git and still sees its hooks and config read-only, and name what it doesn’t: run devvm restart then. If devvm’s own process that runs the VM ends, the VM ends with it at once, as if you pulled its power, so it never runs without the view.

Because a lock in the VM’s view covers one name of a file, devvm also watches .git as a Linux host without locks does, and names what changed at each launch that finds the VM stopped and at devvm stop. That includes your own changes, such as a git remote add or git push -u.

When git on this machine replaces a locked file

The VM sees your changes, because its view is the same folder. A git command on this machine that writes .git/config, such as git config, git remote add or git push -u, writes a new file and renames it over the old one, and the new file isn’t read-only in the VM until devvm locks it again. devvm watches the folders of what it locks, so it locks the new file within milliseconds, but until then the VM can change it, replace it with a file of its own, which devvm then locks as yours, or open it to write it later, which the lock doesn’t stop. A VM running code that watches for that moment can use it, so this is a real gap whenever you change a locked file on this machine while the VM runs.

devvm doesn’t stop it, but it names it:

  • At devvm stop, or at the next launch when the VM stopped another way, devvm names each file it locked again, once however often it happened, and the watch names each one whose contents changed.
  • If devvm couldn’t record whether its locks held while the VM ran, it says so then, and you should check .git’s hooks and config yourself.

Check what it names before you run git in the folder, or stop the VM before you change its .git on this machine.

Hard links

A lock in the VM’s view covers one name of a file, and macOS’s flag covers the file itself, whatever its names. So devvm doesn’t start a VM whose .git/config, or a hook in a locked hooks folder, has another name (a hard link), because the VM could change the file through that other name. Make it a file of its own, by copying it and moving the copy over it, and start the VM again. A file that gets another name while the VM runs isn’t locked again, and devvm names it when the VM stops.

What else differs in the VM

Two more things work differently in the VM. The VM sees .git as a file system of its own, so renaming a file between the working tree and .git fails with Invalid cross-device link, which mv handles by copying the file, and git never does. And the VM can’t remove or rename a submodule’s git folder, so git submodule absorbgitdirs, or rm -rf on a submodule, fails while the VM runs.

A VM that a devvm without these locks made on this machine stays off, and each launch says that devvm can lock it now: run devvm git-protect on to lock it, or devvm git-protect off to keep it off and stop the warning.

When Linux can’t lock

The locks need a kernel that lets a program make a user namespace and mount in it, which Debian, Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE and Arch do by default. Where the kernel doesn’t, devvm doesn’t lock .git, and it watches it instead. devvm doctor says why, and what lets devvm lock:

  • AppArmor, on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, lets only programs that a profile names use a user namespace (Ubuntu).
  • kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone is 0, as on Arch’s linux-hardened kernel. sudo sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1 lets devvm lock, until the next boot unless you set it in /etc/sysctl.d/.
  • user.max_user_namespaces is 0, which sudo sysctl user.max_user_namespaces=15000 changes.

Without the locks, VMs get off as their mode, devvm refuses devvm git-protect on, and --clone keeps the VM out of .git instead, so use it for any repo where you don’t trust what runs in the VM. A VM that’s on, made when the kernel let devvm lock, doesn’t start until it can again, or until you run devvm git-protect off.

Ubuntu

Ubuntu 23.10 and newer set kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns to 1, so a program gets a user namespace with the rights to mount in it only when an AppArmor profile names the program with the userns rule. Ubuntu does that to keep programs that don’t need one out of the kernel code behind it. devvm’s binary lives in a folder you can write, such as ~/.local/lib/devvm/, and a profile for that path would let any program running as you put itself there and get the same rights, which undoes what Ubuntu set the restriction for. So devvm doesn’t ask for a profile, and on Ubuntu with the restriction on it doesn’t lock .git: it watches it, and devvm doctor and each launch say so. Use --clone there for any repo where you don’t trust what runs in the VM.

The warning at each launch

On a Linux host that can’t lock, each launch of a VM that mounts a folder with a .git, or with nested repos, warns that the VM can change their hooks and config, which run on this machine, and names the nested repos devvm doesn’t watch. That includes the launch that creates the VM, and launches of a VM that’s already running. Once you’ve read the warning and decided to go on without protection, run devvm git-protect off in the folder. devvm records that you chose it and stops warning for that VM, but it still names the changes that the next section describes. A VM that you create with --no-git-protect doesn’t warn either, and a --clone VM never warns, because it mounts no .git.

When devvm names a change

On a Linux host that can’t lock, devvm can’t stop the VM from changing .git, and on one that locks, the VM can change a file that git on this machine replaced, but devvm notices the change afterwards on both. When devvm creates a VM, it records a hash of each of these:

  • each path that a lock would cover on macOS, which are the hooks in .git/hooks, .git/config and the rest of what’s locked, submodules’ and nested repos’ included
  • .git/commondir, whether it’s there or not
  • what the config hands over to the project folder: the files that an include.path leads to, and the hooks folder that core.hooksPath names, such as husky’s .husky

Each launch that finds the VM stopped, and devvm stop, hash them again and name every path that changed since the last check, such as .git/config and .git/hooks/pre-commit. A warning names ten paths at most, and then how many more changed. The same checks report what a lock can’t stop either, as they do on macOS: a .git that was replaced, a commondir, a repo or submodule that appeared, and includes, hook links and a core.hooksPath into the project folder (not covered). A launch of a VM that’s already running checks nothing, so run devvm stop when you want the check. A VM that devvm has no hashes for yet, such as one that an older devvm made, records them at its first check and names nothing.

devvm names a change only after it happened, so git on this machine may already have run a changed hook or read a changed config. devvm can’t tell who made a change, so it also names your own, such as a git remote add or git push -u that you ran on this machine. When it names a path that you didn’t change, check it before you run git in the folder:

  • git config --list --show-origin shows each setting of the repo and the file it comes from. Look for settings that run a program, such as core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, filter.* and include.path.
  • ls -la .git/hooks lists the hooks, and git runs a hook there by its name, such as pre-commit, so read every file whose name doesn’t end in .sample.

If you find something that you didn’t put there, remove it, and use --clone for that repo.

What the watch can’t see

The watch isn’t a security boundary, and it doesn’t stop anything. It compares what’s in .git when the VM is stopped with what was there at the last check, so it misses a change that the VM made and then undid before it stopped, even though git on this machine may have run the change in between. It also can’t fully watch some paths, and it names them at every check until they’re gone:

  • A symlink, or a path under one, such as a hook that’s a symlink, or a .git that’s a symlink. devvm never follows a symlink out of the project folder, so it can’t see changes to what such a link points to. For a link that stays inside the project folder, it hashes what the link leads to as well.
  • A file larger than 16 MiB, which devvm records by its size, inode and change time, so it notices a change that keeps the size but can’t hash the file.
  • A hooks folder with more than 1,000 entries, which devvm records by its count and change time. It always hashes the hooks that git runs, at the folder’s top, before the rest. The VM can fill a hooks folder to blind the watch, the folder’s own or a nested repo’s, so devvm names such a folder at every check.
  • What’s past 2,000 paths in all, across every git folder and hooks folder of the folder’s own repo, or past 200 paths of each nested repo.

A repo rarely has any of these, so when devvm names one that you didn’t make, check what it holds, and use --clone for that repo.

item.title: Attack vectors
item.description:
This page lists the common ways that code you didn’t write gets to run on a developer’s machine or gets data off it, and what devvm does about each one. devvm stops most of them on its own, and the habits close most of what’s left. Narrowed, not closed and Left to you are the one list of what devvm leaves open, and each entry links to the page that explains its mechanism.

How devvm handles each attack

The rest of this page sorts the attacks by how much of each one devvm stops:
Blocked The attack can’t work, because what it’s after isn’t in the VM or the VM can’t reach it.
Kept inside the VM The attacker’s code runs, but it runs in the VM, where it reaches only the project folder and what you gave the VM.
Narrowed, not closed devvm closes part of the attack, and the entry says what’s still open.
Left to you devvm doesn’t stop the attack, and the entry says what to do instead.

Some protections hold only on some network tiers or only on macOS, and each entry names its conditions. Everything here rests on the VM’s boundary. How devvm does each of these is in the security model.

Blocked

Credentials on this machine

  • SSH keys. Malware on a developer’s machine looks in ~/.ssh first, because a private key opens every server and repo that trusts it. A VM never mounts ~/.ssh, and besides the project folder it mounts only the shared tools and the folders of devvm’s agent store, read-only, so there’s no key in it to copy. Agent forwarding, which you turn on yourself, lets the VM use your keys but never copy them.
  • Cloud, cluster and registry logins. Worms that steal credentials collect ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.azure, ~/.kube/config, ~/.docker/config.json and the npm publish token in ~/.npmrc. A VM mounts none of them, so a package that goes looking finds nothing. Secrets you keep in the project folder are a different case, which Left to you covers.
  • The Keychain, browsers and password managers. Stealers read saved passwords, cookies and login sessions from browser profiles and the Keychain. The VM has no browser profile of yours, and it can’t reach this machine’s Keychain.
  • Your coding agents’ history. Agent transcripts hold what you pasted into them, such as secrets and code from other projects. Your history never goes into a VM, and each VM’s own history stays in that VM (coding agents).
  • Secrets, on every tier. Every VM, an open one included, gets a placeholder instead of each secret, such as your GitHub token or Claude Code’s token, and the proxy on this machine puts the real value only into requests for that secret’s own hosts (secrets). A placeholder copied out of the VM is worthless elsewhere, because it ends in a random value of that VM’s own, and an open VM that sends a request around its proxy sends only the placeholder.
    • Another VM, or another user’s program on this machine, can’t spend the secret through the proxy either, because the proxy needs the VM’s own password, which only you can read. A program that runs as you can read it, though, as it can read the rest of your files.
    • Codex and opencode logins and Claude Code’s MCP secrets work the same way, and devvm refreshes OAuth logins on this machine, so a VM never holds a refresh token.

Git running code on this machine

  • Git hooks and config. A VM can write the project folder, so without protection it could add a hook such as .git/hooks/post-checkout, or set a command in .git/config: core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, core.editor, a filter.* or diff.*.textconv driver, a credential.helper or a ! alias. Your next git command on this machine would run it. On macOS, devvm locks hooks and config with a flag that even root in the VM can’t clear, and on Linux it makes them read-only in the VM’s view of the folder (.git protection). A Linux host whose kernel doesn’t let devvm do that, which Left to you covers, has neither.
  • devvm’s own git commands. devvm runs git on this machine itself, for example to read your name and email for the VM, to check a --clone VM’s repo for uncommitted changes, and to fetch from the VM. A VM can write a repo that git on this machine reads, such as the project folder’s on Linux or a repo inside a folder it mounts, so devvm’s git runs none of the programs a repo’s config can name:
    • It turns off the repo’s fsmonitor, its hooks, including those its config defines, and its filters, it never enters a submodule for git status, and it uses no transport but ssh, so git status or a fetch of devvm’s runs nothing that the VM wrote into the repo.
    • It runs no program a repo’s config names to check signatures, and it sees a repo’s real history, whatever replace refs or a grafts file say.
    • It ignores the git variables of the shell you run devvm in, such as GIT_DIR and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, so it never works on another repo or config by mistake, and it never asks you anything (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0).
    • Its fetches reach the VM with ssh in batch mode (-o BatchMode=yes), so the VM’s ssh server can’t ask you for a password. They always connect to that VM itself, whatever host the repo’s config sends them to, accept only the host key devvm pinned for it, and forward neither your agent nor any port.

Getting out over the network, on the allowlist and none tiers

  • Sending data to the attacker’s server. Most attacks end by sending what they stole to a server the attacker runs. A confined VM reaches only its proxy, and on the allowlist tier the proxy allows only the hosts on the VM’s allowlist, and on the none tier only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts. On the internet tier, which a VM is on while it learns the hosts it needs, the proxy allows every public host, the attacker’s included, so this holds only for this machine and your networks. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of the default allowlist on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out (allowlists).
  • DNS tunnelling. An attacker can encode data into names and look them up at a DNS server of their own. A VM sends no DNS queries out of it, because names resolve in the proxy on this machine. The names that tools look up in the VM are answered in the VM, by transparent mode’s dnsmasq, which has no server to ask, and the proxy resolves a name only once the VM’s rules allow it.
  • Services on this machine and your network. Code in a VM could attack what developers leave open on localhost, such as databases, dev servers, Docker’s API and other VMs’ ports. It could also attack your router, a NAS, or a cloud provider’s metadata service at 169.254.169.254. The proxy refuses this machine’s own addresses and internal ones, such as loopback, private, link-local and CGNAT ranges, unless a rule names the address (the proxy).
  • DNS rebinding and address tricks. A name can resolve to a public address when it’s checked and to an internal one when it’s dialed, and an internal address can hide in an IPv6 or NAT64 form. The proxy dials only the address it checked, and it sees through NAT64 forms (the proxy).
  • Going around the proxy. Root in a VM can change its routes and firewall, but devvm confines the VM from outside it, so nothing in the VM reaches anything but the proxy (confinement). devvm catches a VM started outside devvm, or one given a second network, with the self-check. It stops a VM that gets out through a second network, and it offers to restart one started outside devvm confined, or stops it when there’s no terminal to ask in.

Spreading beyond the VM

  • Your agents’ config. A rogue agent could add a hook to ~/.claude/settings.json or a skill to ~/.claude/skills, so that it runs the next time you use the agent on this machine. devvm mounts the agents’ config folders read-only, which this machine enforces, and copies their files in on every launch, so nothing the VM changes goes back (mounts). Only devvm agent save copies a VM’s settings into devvm’s agent store, for every VM, and it shows what changed and asks first, so read its diff for hooks, MCP servers and plugins you didn’t add (saving a VM’s settings).
  • Other projects and other VMs. Each project folder gets its own VM with its own disk, and a VM mounts only its own project folder. Each VM’s proxy has its own password, so one VM can’t use another’s secrets. A VM reaches a service in another VM only through a link between VMs that you add in its folder, to a port that the other VM’s folder publishes. A link joins the two VMs’ trust, because code in one can often run code in the other through its service, so a VM links only to a VM on its own tier or a stricter one, and nothing in a VM can add a link (links between VMs).
  • Images, layers and devvm itself. Malware could try to make itself permanent by editing an image, a layer script or devvm’s own files. devvm builds images with nothing from this machine mounted, and the shared tools are read-only in every VM. devvm also refuses a project folder that holds its own folders or sits inside them, so a VM can’t reach the layer scripts that every build runs or the files devvm runs on this machine (only the project folder).
  • A folder made again. If you delete a repo and clone another at the same path, the new folder never gets the old VM’s disk or anything left in it. devvm knows a folder by its inode as well as its path, so it refuses and offers devvm rm or devvm adopt (a folder made again).
  • A devcontainer.json that reaches this machine. Other tools run a devcontainer’s initializeCommand on the host. devvm never runs it, refuses ${localEnv:…}, adds no mounts from the file and doesn’t follow a link out of the folder (devcontainer.json). devvm uses the file’s image only when the image’s registry gives it to anyone who asks, and it refuses a registry on this machine or its network. Behind a company proxy, devvm looks the image up through the company proxy and checks only the registry’s name, so a company proxy that reaches this machine or its network for a name that looks public takes the lookup there (the design note).
  • Impersonating a VM. ssh checks a VM against host keys that devvm reads through the VM’s backend instead of over the network, so a program that answers on the VM’s port in its place is refused (ssh access by name).

Kept inside the VM

The attacks in this section run the attacker’s code, and devvm doesn’t stop that code from running. It runs in the VM, as the VM’s user, who has passwordless sudo. From there it reaches the project folder, or with --clone the VM’s own clone of it, and the secrets the VM uses, which are placeholders on every tier. It reaches what the VM’s tier allows: the hosts on the allowlist on the allowlist tier, every public host on the internet tier, and the whole network on the open tier. Everything in Blocked still holds. What the code writes into the project folder can still reach you when a program on this machine runs it, which Left to you covers.

Install and build scripts

  • npm, yarn, pnpm and bun lifecycle scripts. A package’s preinstall, install, postinstall and prepare scripts run any command when the package is installed, and most npm attacks use them. pnpm’s build approvals (pnpm approve-builds) and --ignore-scripts narrow which packages run scripts, and they’re still worth using, but a package you approved runs its scripts all the same, even one compromised after you approved it. In a VM, those scripts reach only what this section’s introduction lists.
  • Python packages. Installing a source distribution runs its setup.py or its build backend, and a .pth file in site-packages runs code every time Python starts.
  • Ruby gems. A gem with a native extension runs its extconf.rb when it’s installed, and Bundler can install gems straight from a git repo.
  • Rust build scripts and procedural macros. build.rs and procedural macros run on cargo build and cargo check, and also when rust-analyzer opens the project, so opening the folder in an editor is enough to run them. With devvm code, VS Code’s extensions, rust-analyzer among them, run in the VM (devvm host and devvm code).
  • Go modules. Go has no install scripts, but cgo passes flags to the C compiler, go generate runs commands, a toolchain line in go.mod makes Go download another toolchain, and a module’s init functions run in every test and program that imports it.
  • Makefiles, task runners and curl | sh. A Makefile, a justfile or a project’s install line from its README runs whatever its author wrote.

Bad packages and images

  • Typosquatting, dependency confusion and made-up names. Attackers publish packages under names one typo away from popular ones, under a company’s internal package names with a higher version, and under names that AI coding agents invent and that attackers then register. Their code runs as the scripts above do.
  • Compromised maintainers. A trusted package can turn malicious when its maintainer’s account is taken over or a new maintainer joins with bad intent, as event-stream (2018) and xz (2024) did. Updating such a package runs its new code in the VM.
  • Malicious images. An image from --from or from a devcontainer’s image runs its own code as root in the build VM (the image is untrusted). devvm uses only images that the registry gives to anyone who asks anonymously, never one that only your Docker or your registry login reaches, and it confines builds (read-only and confined builds). On macOS a build can’t reach this machine’s loopback, but Left to you covers what it still reaches.
  • A devcontainer.json’s commands and features. A project’s postCreateCommand and its other commands run in the VM as the VM’s user, as soon as devvm makes the VM. Its image and features decide what’s in the VM, and devvm adds its ports to the ones it forwards to this machine’s localhost, even beyond a list you narrowed, so the VM is the project’s from the start. Its features can only be devvm’s own layers, so devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script. devvm --no-devcontainer skips the file for a project you don’t trust that far (devcontainer.json).

Rogue agents

  • Prompt injection. Instructions hidden in a README, an issue, a code comment, a web page, a dependency’s docs or an MCP tool’s output can turn a coding agent against you. devvm can’t tell an agent’s own work from injected work, so it limits what the agent reaches instead. An attack like this needs private data, untrusted input and a way to send the data out. On the allowlist tier, the only way out is the hosts on the allowlist, which Left to you covers.
  • Agents with their checks off. An agent run with claude --dangerously-skip-permissions or codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox acts without asking, and a mistaken rm -rf ~ or sudo command reaches only the VM. The project folder is still the agent’s to change, so commit often, or use --clone to keep the agent’s work apart until you fetch it.
  • Malware that stays. Anything the attacker leaves in the VM, such as a cron job, a changed shell startup file or a backdoored program, stays in that VM’s disk and goes into no other VM’s, unless you save an agent’s settings that it changed with devvm agent save. What it wrote into the project folder stays there, though, and the folder’s next VM gets it, such as a devcontainer.json command that runs as soon as devvm makes the VM, or a hook in the project’s agent settings. devvm never deletes a VM on its own, because it may hold unsaved work, so save what you need and run devvm rm, then check the folder for what the VM writes, or use --clone, before you make the VM again.
  • Mining and resource abuse. A VM’s CPUs, memory and disk are capped by its size, which devvm size shows and changes (size). The VM’s proxy on this machine carries at most 1024 tunnels for it at once, but it doesn’t count the VM’s plain HTTP requests in absolute form or its idle kept-alive connections (the proxy).

Narrowed, not closed

Secrets and keys the VM may use

  • Worms that use your GitHub token. Shai-Hulud (2025) spread through npm install scripts. It collected npm, GitHub and cloud credentials, then used them to publish repos and new versions of packages. A VM holds no npm or cloud credentials, and its GitHub token is a placeholder. The proxy still puts the real GitHub token into every request to GitHub’s hosts, so a worm in the VM can push, make repos and do whatever else the GitHub token’s scope allows. Use a fine-grained GitHub token scoped to the repos the VM needs, or bind none (saving and binding secrets).
  • A host that sends your secret back. The proxy puts a secret only into requests for its own hosts, but it passes their replies to the VM as they are. A host that echoes a request’s headers, such as a debug endpoint, or an error page that quotes them, shows the VM the real value. This matters most for your own secrets, whose hosts you choose, so give each one only hosts that you trust with it. A secret’s hosts are on the allowlist of every VM that uses it, on every tier, so on a host where anyone can make an account, code in the VM can also send data to an account of its own there.
  • Minting credentials with a secret. A VM that can use a secret can use it to make another credential that outlasts it. The proxy refuses GitHub REST calls that add an SSH key, a deploy key, a self-hosted runner or a webhook with 403, but it can’t refuse everything, such as GitHub’s GraphQL API, an OAuth app grant or other services.
    • A bound API key can make credentials too. With Google Gemini’s key, code in the VM can ask generativelanguage.googleapis.com for an ephemeral token for Gemini’s Live API, which lasts up to about 20 hours and allows as many uses as the VM asks for. With xAI’s key it can ask api.x.ai for a realtime client secret that lasts as long as the VM chooses, and with OpenAI’s key it can ask api.openai.com for one that lasts up to 2 hours.
    • These credentials work without the proxy, and the proxy allows the requests that make them, because opencode’s experimental voice mode makes them itself (API keys the proxy puts in). If a VM may have done this, rotate the secret and check the service’s keys, access tokens and runners.
  • Keys devvm can’t tell apart. devvm takes the keys out of the VM’s copies of your agents’ settings and logins only where it can tell a key from the rest. A key in other text, such as a hook’s command, stays when it neither starts like a known key nor follows Bearer or Basic. opencode’s and pi’s keys that devvm can’t bind, such as a local model server’s, stay on this machine unless you list their provider in config.toml’s [pass-keys], and then they go in as they are. The agents’ folders that the VM mounts whole, such as ~/.claude/skills or ~/.config/opencode/plugin, reach the VM with every file in them, so a .env in one is in the VM, and so is a private plugin marketplace’s git config with a password or an access token in its URL. Keep secrets out of those folders (what stays in the VM’s copies).
  • Your SSH agent. While agent forwarding is on, anything in the VM can use the agent’s keys to push or log in to servers, though it can’t copy them. The VM has the agent while you’re connected. devvm ssh-agent devvm limits it to the keys you add to devvm’s own agent, and an agent that asks you to approve each use, such as 1Password’s or Secretive, narrows it further.

Git

  • The shell prompt. Many shell prompts and editors run git status as soon as you cd into a folder or open it, and git status runs core.fsmonitor. Where devvm locks .git, the lock covers the .git of the folder and of the nested repos devvm has found, so opening the folder runs nothing that the VM wrote into them. It doesn’t cover a submodule the VM adds, a .git the VM replaces or a repo the VM makes while it runs, which git on this machine reads before devvm’s next check, as the entries below describe.
  • Submodules with their own config. The VM writes .git/index to commit, so it can add a submodule whose config sets core.fsmonitor. git status, git diff, git add -A and git describe --dirty on this machine read that config, and run what it names, before devvm stops the VM or the next launch finds the submodule and locks it. No git setting keeps git on this machine out of a submodule that the VM adds, because the VM writes the .gitmodules file that git reads, and several commands enter a submodule whatever the settings say. So use --clone for a repo where you run git on this machine while the VM runs (not covered).
  • Replacing .git. The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, or add a commondir that points git at another config. devvm reports these on each launch but doesn’t prevent them, so check what it names before you run git in the folder (what a lock can’t stop).
  • Nested repos. devvm protects the git repos nested in the folder, but the VM can clone a new one while it runs, or move a protected one aside and put another in its place, and git on this machine runs its config before devvm’s next check names it. devvm also doesn’t protect a nested repo deeper than four folders, in a folder such as node_modules, or past the first 100, which it counts and names (nested repos).

Network

  • Domain fronting. The proxy checks the host name that a TLS connection asks for, its SNI, but not the Host inside the encrypted traffic, so a CDN that serves many sites on one address can route an allowed connection to a site that isn’t allowed. The proxy reads the connections to hosts with a bound secret, and it refuses a request in them that names another host. A connection that transparent mode sends to the proxy is judged by its SNI in the same way, and so is a client with an Encrypted Client Hello configuration from somewhere other than DNS, whose outer SNI, the CDN’s public name, is what the proxy sees. The VM’s own names give no client such a configuration.
  • The first seconds of an open start. A VM that was confined and is made open runs transparent mode from its next boot until that launch’s setup takes it out, a few seconds later. In that window, its names resolve to the stand-in address and its connections reach its proxy, which is an open one by then, so they reach what the open tier allows, and nothing keeps those answers after.
  • Model providers that fetch for the VM. The proxy allows a bound API key’s provider hosts on port 443, and some providers’ own tools fetch URLs that the request names, such as Google Gemini’s URL context and Search grounding, xAI’s live search, Groq’s compound models and Mistral’s agents with web search, as Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s web fetch and search tools do. Code in the VM can send data out through such a tool to a host that the allowlist doesn’t have (API keys the proxy puts in).
  • Ports the VM listens on. devvm forwards the VM’s TCP ports from 1024 up to this machine’s localhost, unless you list the ports with --ports, so a VM could take a port that a program on this machine trusts while that port is free, and what the VM serves there reaches whatever connects to it. devvm’s forwarder never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, or one that devvm records for a VM, but a program that binds a port on all addresses after devvm forwarded it gets its localhost connections sent to the VM. devvm ports limits what a VM forwards, and devvm ports none forwards nothing, though a project’s devcontainer.json adds its forwardPorts to that list when devvm makes the VM or devvm update reads the file (devcontainer.json, ports, port forwarding).
  • VS Code’s relays. Over Remote-SSH, which devvm code opens, VS Code forwards the ports that programs in the VM listen on, and it answers git’s prompts with your GitHub sign-in. devvm turns both off in the VM’s VS Code settings each time it sets the VM up, but the VM can turn them back on, so turn them off in your own VS Code settings as well (VS Code).
  • What a VM does through a link. A link between VMs joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the service it reaches, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has the target’s network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. devvm limits a link to the ports the target publishes, on the target’s loopback, and a client to targets on its own tier or a stricter one, but it doesn’t limit what the service does. In a group, every VM trusts every other in the same way, and a VM that joins later gets the same reach (links between VMs).
  • History imported from a less strict tier. An export of agents’ history carries what the old VM’s agents read, so importing one from an open VM into a VM on the allowlist tier can bring in credentials and data that the new VM couldn’t reach itself, along with any instructions planted in them. devvm warns before such an import, and before importing an export whose tier it has no record of, but it imports all the same. Import history only from a VM you trusted as much as the new one (importing history).
  • What one VM learns of another through the shared Nix cache. VMs with the nix layer share one cache of Nix’s packages on this machine. A VM can tell by how fast the cache answers whether some VM fetched a public package. The packages are public, and a project’s flake.lock names the ones it needs, so this tells a VM only that another project on this machine uses a package. A VM that fetches many packages can also fill the cache up to its cap and push other VMs’ packages out, so they download them again, but it can’t fill the disk past the cap or keep anything that cache.nixos.org didn’t sign (the shared Nix cache).
  • Through a company proxy. The company proxy looks up the names it’s sent itself, and it may get another answer than this machine did, or a later one, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to there. Under a name that an allowlist names, a VM reaches whatever the company proxy reaches, such as your company’s internal hosts and the company proxy’s own host, which is this machine’s loopback when the company proxy runs on this machine, as a VPN client’s does. A name that the VM’s allowlist doesn’t allow never reaches the company proxy (the design note).
  • Which names resolve to internal addresses. When the proxy refuses a name because this machine’s lookup gives it an internal address, its refusal says so, so a VM can learn which names this machine’s DNS resolves to internal addresses. The refusal never names the address, this machine’s DNS server or the company proxy, which stay in the proxy’s own log (log files).

This machine

  • A nested project replaced through its parent folder’s VM. A project with a VM of its own inside a folder with another VM is in both VMs, so code in the parent folder’s VM can replace the nested project folder with a link, such as one to your home folder, which the nested VM would mount at its next start.
    • devvm warns each time it makes or opens such a nested VM, naming the parent folder’s VM. It checks the nested folder, by its path and by the folder itself, just before it starts the nested VM and again once the VM runs, and it refuses the start or stops the VM again when the folder was replaced.
    • On macOS the VM mounts the folder itself rather than its path, so it never mounts what a link points to, even when the folder is put back before devvm checks again.
    • On Linux the VM mounts the folder by its path, so code that replaces the folder for the moment the VM’s backend mounts it and puts it back before devvm checks again stays unseen, and the VM keeps what the link pointed to until its next start. Keep a nested project that you don’t want the parent folder’s VM to reach out of the parent folder (a nested project replaced).
  • Set-id files on Linux hosts. Root in a VM can set the set-user-id bit on a file in the project folder, and on Linux hosts that bit reaches the host, so the file runs as its owner for whoever runs it. devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, but not at a launch into a running VM, and Troubleshooting says how to clear them. Don’t run programs from the project folder outside the VM (set-id files).
  • The proxy’s CA keys. Inside a VM, its CA vouches for any site, so someone with a copy of its key and a place on your network could impersonate sites to that VM. Each VM has CAs of its own, so a copy reaches one VM and no other. Only you can read the keys, they never leave this machine, and devvm keeps them out of Time Machine. Each CA lasts 30 days, so a copy goes stale, but the next CA’s key is on disk for up to 23 days before that CA starts, so a copy of it taken then works until that CA ends, up to 53 days later. Keep ~/.local/share/devvm/vms out of other backup and sync tools as well, and on Linux, which has no Time Machine, out of your backups (the VM’s CA).
  • Your company proxy’s password. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings: an open VM goes through its own proxy, which goes through the company proxy for it.
    • devvm keeps the password out of its run logs only where it can tell it’s a password, so one in an address with neither a scheme nor a port, one with a raw /, ?, # or @ in it, or one in a run of more than 4 KiB without a space that a command writes in pieces can stay.
    • Lima’s own log for the VM holds the password until the VM has started, when devvm replaces it with as many *, so the log still shows its length. If devvm is killed before then, or you run limactl start outside devvm, the log keeps it. With config.toml’s proxy, the mise that devvm runs on this machine gets the password in its environment, where programs that run as you can read it (open VMs and builds, the run log).

Left to you

Files the VM writes

The VM can write anything in the project folder, and devvm locks only .git. Any other file there that a program on this machine runs, or reads as its config, is the VM’s to change. --clone keeps all of these away from this machine until you fetch the VM’s work and review it.

  • Hooks in the working tree. Hooks kept in the project, such as husky’s .husky/ with core.hooksPath pointing there, run on this machine, and so do an include.path or a hook symlink that leads into the folder. devvm warns about them when it makes the VM (not covered).
  • Agent config in the project. Claude Code reads a project’s .claude/settings.json, whose hooks run commands, and .mcp.json, which starts MCP servers, and agents follow a project’s CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. pi reads a project’s .pi folder, whose extensions run as code when pi starts, whose settings.json installs packages and sets shellCommandPrefix, which comes before every command pi runs, and whose mcp.json starts MCP servers. pi asks before it loads them, unless your ~/.pi/agent/trust.json on this machine already trusts the folder or your settings trust every folder. Running an agent on this machine in the folder after the VM has worked in it runs what the VM wrote, so run your agents in the VM.
  • Editor and tool config. VS Code runs .vscode/tasks.json tasks set to runOn: folderOpen and starts the interpreters and formatters that .vscode/settings.json names. direnv loads .envrc, and mise reads mise.toml’s environment, hooks and tasks. Keep VS Code’s workspace trust on, and use direnv’s and mise’s own approval prompts.
  • Project code and binaries. npm install, make, a test run or ./bin/tool on this machine runs whatever the VM wrote. Run them in the VM instead.
  • Symlinks out of the folder. The VM can create a link in the project folder that points at a file of yours, such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. A program on this machine that follows it, such as an upload, an archive or an agent reading files, reads your file instead. devvm itself never follows a link out of the folder.
  • Backdoors in code you merge. Treat the VM’s commits as an untrusted contributor’s, and review them before you merge, deploy or publish them.
  • Secrets in the project folder. A .env file, a project .npmrc or a cloud key in the folder is in the VM. On the allowlist tier it can reach only the hosts on the allowlist, on the internet tier any public host, and on the open tier anywhere. Keep secrets out of the project folder, or use --clone, which copies no untracked files into the VM but those of a git stash -u entry, though it copies your repo’s hooks as they are and a folder of repos’ own files (what’s copied). The same goes for your agents’ config folders, which keys devvm can’t tell apart covers (mounts).
  • What you paste in. An image, a PDF or a file you send with devvm paste is a file in the VM, which anything in the VM can read, as it reads the project folder. devvm reads only an image, a PDF or a copied file’s reference from your clipboard, never text, asks before sending a copied file, showing its path, refuses a link anywhere in a copied file’s path but the system’s own, and lets nothing the VM says onto your clipboard, so paste nothing you wouldn’t put in the folder (pasting images).

The network

  • Allowed hosts. Anything an allowed host accepts can carry data out. github.com accepts a push from anyone with an account, including an attacker with an account of their own, and the npm registry accepts packages the same way. Keep allowlists short, narrow a host to the methods and paths a VM needs (rules by method and path), and check what a VM reached with devvm network log. A rule by method and path judges each request’s method and path, not its body or its other headers, so what an allowed request sends still reaches the host. A deny of git-receive-pack on github.com, for example, blocks pushes over HTTPS alone: a push over ssh to github.com:22, if a rule allows it, and the commits that GitHub’s Git Data API makes at api.github.com with a GitHub token go on.
  • What your secrets allow. A VM can push with a GitHub token it may use and spend Claude quota. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, bind only the secrets a VM needs, and deny the methods a VM mustn’t use, such as devvm network deny api.github.com --method POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE.
  • Open VMs. An open VM, because you chose open or passed --network open, reaches everything this machine can, including its services on localhost, such as other VMs’ ports, dev servers and databases, and your local network, directly and through its proxy, which applies no rules for it. Its proxy still puts its secrets in, so it can spend them on their hosts as any VM can, but it holds only their placeholders, as every VM does. A VM started outside devvm, such as with limactl start, or one running since before devvm network gave it a confined tier, runs unconfined in the same way until devvm restarts it confined (the self-check).
  • Your browser. Programs in a VM can open URLs in this machine’s browser, and a page that a VM serves on a forwarded port runs in your browser like any other. From there it can reach the internet past the VM’s tier, and your services on localhost. Browsers send a host’s cookies to every port on it, so a server in the VM on a forwarded localhost port gets the cookies of the apps you use on localhost, such as a local dashboard you’re signed in to.
  • Remote forwards you add. A RemoteForward in your ssh config, or an ssh -R you type, makes this machine connect to whatever it names for the VM. devvm’s ssh entries can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours without also refusing an ssh -R you type. The VM’s ssh server refuses a remote forward on any address outside 127.77.0.0/16, the range devvm keeps for links between VMs, so one on the VM’s localhost, which ssh -R asks for by default, is refused. Root in the VM can change that setting, though, and the server allows a forward on an address in 127.77.0.0/16 for anyone it lets in. A forward you ask for by a host name that begins with 127.77. binds whatever address that name resolves to in the VM. So keep remote forwards out of Host *, and don’t forward into a VM you don’t trust (ssh into VMs).
  • A company CA you add. A company CA that you put in ~/.config/devvm/ca can read the TLS traffic of every VM, whatever its tier, as it can this machine’s, and the proxy trusts it for its own connections. Only that folder adds CAs to the proxy, and nothing a VM sends can.

The platform

  • .git on Linux hosts. devvm makes hooks and config read-only in the VM’s view, but a git command on this machine that replaces .git/config while the VM runs leaves the new file the VM’s to change, replace or open for writing until devvm locks it again, which devvm names only when the VM stops (when git replaces a locked file). Where the kernel doesn’t let devvm use a user namespace, such as on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, VMs have no .git protection, and the VM can change hooks and config that run on the host, so use --clone there (Linux hosts).
  • What a build reaches. A build, such as a --from image’s or a layer’s, reaches the internet and your local network as well, this machine’s own address on it included, so a service of yours that listens on every address is in its reach. On macOS that’s all it reaches of this machine, because its loopback is out of reach, but on Linux the build reaches the services on this machine’s localhost too, such as other VMs’ proxies and dev servers. Build images only from container images and layers you trust (confinement).
  • Escaping the VM. A bug in Lima, Apple’s Virtualization framework or QEMU could let code out of the VM. So could a bug in devvm’s own programs on this machine that read what a VM sends, which are the VM’s proxy, the port forwarder, the sessions of links between VMs, devvm agent save and the export of agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save.
